\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

The design, the population and the decision rules were fixed before any number
was read, and they are stated here as they were registered, so the results can
be read against a fixed target rather than a moving one.
One of the four registered experiments has now run.
\Cref{sec:experiments:law} reports it, and reports it against the rules in the
order they were written --- including the two places where those rules turned
out not to be answerable in the form they were posed.
E2, E3 and E4 remain unmeasured and every quantity in them is marked as such,
with the instrument that will produce it named in place.
The de-risk pilot of \cref{sec:experiments:pilot} is a separate case: it is
measured under a deprecated configuration and quoted with that disclaimer
rather than silently refreshed.

\subsection{The paired population}
\label{sec:experiments:population}

The comparison needs the same theorem on all three channels with a genuine
natural-language \emph{proof} rather than a problem statement, which is scarcer
than it looks:
a corpus pairing an informal statement with a formal statement pins down no
argument on either side.
We join a formal corpus carrying complete human-annotated Lean proofs against a
natural-language corpus carrying complete worked solutions, on problem text.
\Cref{tab:roster} fixes the candidates.
Statement banks with Lean formalisations are plentiful, but rows carrying a
complete \emph{worked} solution alongside a kernel-checkable formal side are
scarce --- of the roster only ProofNet pairs a natural-language proof with a
formal statement natively --- and where a formal side must be produced rather
than joined, a statement autoformaliser supplies it with the kernel and a
faithfulness check downstream \citep{wang2025kimina, lin2025goedelprover,
gao2025herald}.
Two facts are declared before any result.
Each row carries whether its formal proof and its solution are human-authored or
machine-generated, and strata are never pooled silently.
And question type is stratified, because competition corpora mix goals that ask
for a proof with goals that ask for a number, the latter formalising into
decision-procedure calls whose cost says nothing about reasoning;
grade-school word problems are carried as an explicitly degenerate control with
\emph{opposite} pre-registered predictions, so the control discriminates rather
than illustrates.

\tbm{the full selection cascade as a table: source rows, rows with a
proof-bearing formal witness, join rate under whitespace and alphanumeric
normalisation, rows whose natural-language field is a derivation rather than a
statement, rows surviving decontamination, and the final matched set, with
difficulty statistics at every stage so the reader can see which way the cascade
selects; instrument: the join and audit scripts, published}

\subsection{E0 --- the de-risk pilot, and its disclaimer}
\label{sec:experiments:pilot}

One measurement predates this pre-registration and is what de-risks it;
we quote it with its flaws stated rather than hold it back.
Under an earlier configuration of the term pipeline --- since deprecated, which
is why every number here is de-risk evidence and none is a result --- the
per-theorem surprisal of held-out declarations was:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
nats/theorem & median & IQR & mean & p90 & p99 & max \\
\midrule
proof term (\(H_{\mathrm{value}}\)) &
  3.10 & 0.90--10.50 & 10.15 & 25.1 & 93.4 & 1035.3 \\
statement (\(H_{\mathrm{type}}\)) &
  16.42 & 14.46--20.34 & 18.88 & 27.5 & 52.0 & 349.1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Mathematical prose runs of order \(10^{0}\) nats per token
\citep{shannon1951prediction, brown1992estimate, deletang2024compression}, so a
\(10^{2}\)--\(10^{3}\)-token worked solution costs \(10^{2}\)--\(10^{4}\) nats
per theorem --- an estimate, not a measured distribution.
No published figure is the per-token cross-entropy of mathematical prose as
such, so we say what stands behind the order of magnitude.
\Citet{gao2020pile} report test bits per byte on an arXiv component falling
from \(1.35\) to \(0.77\) across model scale, which is \(0.53\) nats per byte
and, at a byte-per-token ratio we supply rather than measure, of order one nat
per token;
that component is \LaTeX{} source across all fields rather than prose, and the
conversion is ours.
The predecessor to this work measured arXiv abstracts at \(1.73\) nats per
token against \(2.79\) on general text, teacher-forced and per token, under a
configuration this paper otherwise deprecates.
The re-run at the current pin is part of the registered programme.
The pilot's role is confined to pricing \(\CE_{\mathrm{FL}}\) in
\cref{eq:mathcap}:
it says the experiment is worth running, not that the conclusion holds.

\subsection{E1 --- one scaling law per channel}
\label{sec:experiments:law}

This is the instrument the title's claim rests on, and it has now run.
For each channel we train a from-scratch grid over model size and data and fit
\cref{eq:chinchilla} on total parameters, under one functional form, one
fitting procedure and one grid design.
The arms are from scratch rather than fine-tuned (R1) because a pretrained body
imports an unknown quantity of the very data the fit is about.
All three arms are built and measured:
\num{sweep/term/sizes} model sizes against \num{sweep/term/dlevels} data rungs
per channel, \num{sweep/term/cells} cells on each arm and \(60\) in all, every
cell scored on the same \(17{,}566\) held-out theorems of one frozen
population.
Because the three vocabularies differ by \(8\times\), the total-parameter
ladders differ per channel --- \num{sweep/term/nlo}M to \num{sweep/term/nhi}M
on term, \num{sweep/surf/nlo}M to \num{sweep/surf/nhi}M on surface,
\num{sweep/nl/nlo}M to \num{sweep/nl/nhi}M on English --- while on the
non-embedding axis all three arms are the \emph{same} seven models,
\num{sweep/term/nelo}M to \num{sweep/term/nehi}M.
We report the exponent on both axes throughout and quote neither alone, because
an embedding parameter buys less capacity than a block parameter and the
embedding's share of \(N\) is channel-dependent, which inflates \(\alpha\) most
where the vocabulary is largest \citep{porian2024resolving}.
This is not a hypothetical: \citet{pearce2024reconciling} attribute much of the
Kaplan--Chinchilla exponent discrepancy to non-embedding counting \emph{combined
with analysis at small scale}, and our ladder sits squarely in that regime, so
the convention is predicted to move the answer here rather than merely permitted
to.
It does.
The data axis is delivered tokens, never the nominal budget, which overstates
them by up to a fifth.

\paragraph{One result comes before the decision rules, because it limits what
they can be applied to.}
The term channel is measured \emph{outside} the functional family of
\cref{eq:chinchilla} along the rung this grid varies --- which is a data rung
and an optimiser-update rung at once, and the distinction is taken up below.
At a fixed model size, three delivered-\(D\) budgets pin that rung
with nothing left to estimate --- no prior, no \(\alpha\), no floor --- and the
term arm's loss comes out \emph{concave} in \(\log D\).
Since \(E_c\) and \(A_c N^{-\alpha_c}\) are both non-negative,
\cref{eq:chinchilla} is necessarily \emph{convex} in \(\log D\) at every
parameter value, so the observed curvature is not a poor fit but an impossible
one;
the two properties are equivalent, and steepening is available only at a
negative constant.
At \(53.6\)M parameters the concavity is
\num{sweep/term/n54/concavity}, which is
\num{sweep/term/n54/concavityz} standard deviations from zero.
The test is closed form --- the concavity is linear in the log losses, so its
standard deviation is exact rather than simulated --- and its noise scale is
borrowed from the healthy arms' fit residual, which conflates measurement noise
with the form being right.
We therefore quote what that borrowing would have to be worth: term's own
run-to-run scatter would have to be
\num{sweep/term/n54/concavitybreakevenratio}\(\times\) the measured value
before this became a chance result.

\paragraph{What this licenses, and the confound that bounds it.}
Two readings of the curvature have to be kept apart, and an earlier revision of
this section ran them together.
\emph{The curvature does not refuse the joint fit.}
Under the prior in force the term arm's joint route is accepted, at
\(R^2 = \num{sweep/term/rsq}\) over \num{sweep/term/cellsused} cells, and its
exponents are reported from it.
A previous revision estimated the term exponent from the arm's fixed-\(D\)
slope instead, on the ground that the joint route returned an \(\alpha\) below
that slope --- an arithmetic contradiction under \(f = 1\) rather than a weak
result.
That was a symptom of a prior--data conflict and never a measurement: under a
data-exponent prior centred at \(0.298\) with the minimum width, the posterior
came back no tighter than the prior itself, so the fit was pinned where the data
did not want it and the misfit along that rung pushed \(\alpha\) down.
The slope is in any case the wrong estimator on this arm, for the same reason
the curvature exists --- the bound \(\lvert \mathrm{d} \log L / \mathrm{d} \log
N \rvert \le \alpha\) needs a non-negative constant, and where the constant is
negative the slope \emph{overstates} \(\alpha\).
\emph{What the curvature does refuse is the family.}
The fitted law misses its own cells by \num{sweep/term/relrms}\% on this arm
against \num{sweep/surf/relrms}\% and \num{sweep/nl/relrms}\% on the other two,
and the residuals are signed by rung rather than scattered --- which is what a
wrong functional form looks like and what a noisy one does not.
\emph{Reading the curvature as a statement about the data direction is a
further step, and this grid does not license it.}
The rungs vary \(D\) by varying the number of optimiser steps at fixed
tokens-per-step, so data and optimisation are collinear by construction;
at fixed batch and schedule the data axis \emph{is} the summed-learning-rate
axis \citep{tissue2025annealing}, and the step term of
\citet[\S5]{kaplan2020scaling} is a second law our three points cannot be
separated from.
Its \emph{magnitude}, at least, is not the issue.
An excess loss from under-training that is linear in \(\log D\) cancels
identically from a second difference, whatever its size, so no amount of
uniform starvation can manufacture curvature;
only a \emph{change} in the return to successive step increases can, and the
sign of that change decides the sign of the bias.
Where returns diminish --- the asymptotic regime --- the excess falls more
across the low pair than the high and the measurement \emph{understates} the
curvature.
Where they accelerate, it overstates it, and that window was real rather than
hypothetical: early training runs a plateau before the drop, and our shortest
rung is a few dozen optimiser steps behind a handful of warmup steps.
\emph{So we measured the direction instead of assuming one.}
The quantity that settles it is the ratio of the returns to two successive step
increases, which cells holding \(D\) fixed across \emph{three} step counts read
directly --- two would not, a line having no curvature to find --- and the
shortest rung admits a third count exactly, at four times and four times again,
delivering its siblings' token total to the token.
The second quadrupling of steps buys markedly less than the first, so the
penalty diminishes rather than accelerates: it falls on the far side of the
value at which it would cancel, and outside the window that would have made this
result an artefact of the grid.
Only the \emph{sign} of that comparison is claimed here, and deliberately.
The three step counts are scored on the in-loop per-token loss rather than on
the registered per-theorem observable, and the two are not related by a fixed
factor --- different rows, different token regions --- so the ratio's magnitude
is provisional where its direction is not, and the artefact window lies far
enough away that the direction settles the question on its own.
Substituting that measured penalty rather than an assumed one leaves the
data-limited curve \emph{more} concave than the raw measurement, not less.
The step confound was suppressing this finding rather than manufacturing it,
and \num{sweep/term/n54/concavity} is a lower bound on the departure.

\paragraph{Pre-registered decision rules, in order.}
\emph{(i) The unit trap, first, because it is the one that can manufacture the
result.}
Each fitted floor is converted by that channel's tokens-per-theorem before any
comparison.
If the predicted ordering holds per token but not per theorem, we report that we
have measured our tokenizers, and the claim fails.
\emph{(ii) The floors.}
We predict \(E_{\mathrm{NL}} > E_{\mathrm{surface}} > E_{\mathrm{term}}\) in
nats per theorem;
a non-monotone ordering, or an interval on any adjacent pair containing zero, is
a negative result and is reported as one.
\emph{(iii) The model exponents, and the affine form.}
\Cref{eq:alphafibre} predicts \(\alpha_{\mathrm{term}} >
\alpha_{\mathrm{surface}} > \alpha_{\mathrm{NL}}\), and more than the ordering:
that the \emph{reciprocals} are affine in the fibre each rendering adds, so with
the term channel as the zero-fibre reference the gaps
\(1/\alpha_{\mathrm{surface}} - 1/\alpha_{\mathrm{term}}\) and
\(1/\alpha_{\mathrm{NL}} - 1/\alpha_{\mathrm{term}}\) estimate
\(d_{\mathrm{form}}/\kappa\) for the two renderings and must both be positive.
We report the implied dimensions beside the exponents.
\emph{We register no prediction for \(\beta\)}:
\cref{eq:alphafibre} is a statement about the model exponent, and the published
fits already show \(\beta\) nearly unmoved where \(\alpha\) moves a great deal
(\cref{sec:method:scaling}).
A \(\beta\) ordering, should we see one, is an observation and not a
confirmation.
\emph{(iv) The cross-check between instruments.}
By \cref{prop:floor} a channel's floor is its signal plus its noise, and
\cref{eq:mathcap} caps the signal independently, so the fitted floor ratio and
the measured \(\CE_{\mathrm{FL}}/\CE_{\mathrm{NL}}\) of
\cref{sec:experiments:cap} are two routes to one quantity.
We publish both;
if they disagree beyond their intervals, the functional form is wrong on at
least one channel and we say so rather than pick the flattering one.
\emph{(v) The dial test, which is what discriminates this theory.}
On a synthetic arm whose English side is written by a generator we hold, the
fibre is ours to set:
raising the generator's temperature adds fibre \emph{entropy} at roughly fixed
structure, while widening its style repertoire adds fibre \emph{dimension} at
roughly fixed entropy.
\Cref{sec:method:scaling} predicts that the first moves \(E\) and leaves
\(\alpha\), and that the second moves \(\alpha\).
Any account on which noise is a single scalar predicts both dials move both
terms, so this is the comparison that separates the fibre theory from its
competitors --- and it needs no human corpus, only compute.
\tbm{fitted \((E,\alpha)\) at each setting of the two dials, with the generator
and its sampling parameters published; instrument: the synthetic-English
generator and the same grid and fitting routine as the main arms}
\emph{(vi)} No floor's \emph{value} is read as an entropy, on any channel.

\paragraph{The outcome, against those rules in the same order.}
\emph{(i) The unit trap fires, and it is not a near miss.}
The three channels order one way per theorem --- English
\num{sweep/nl/ce}, term \num{sweep/term/ce}, surface \num{sweep/surf/ce} nats
--- and the \emph{opposite} way per token, at \num{sweep/surf/natspertok},
\num{sweep/nl/natspertok} and \num{sweep/term/natspertok} respectively
(\cref{tab:sweep}).
The reason is length: a theorem costs \num{sweep/term/tokperthm} term tokens
against \num{sweep/surf/tokperthm} surface tokens, a factor above two hundred.
Every cross-channel statement in this paper therefore names its denominator,
and a reader should treat one that does not as undefined.
\emph{(ii) The floor ordering cannot be tested as registered, and the quantity
that stands in its place is non-monotone.}
\(E\) is not identified over this grid's \((N,D)\) range --- no arm trains past
two epochs, so the campaign's standing assumption fixes \(E\) at zero rather
than fitting it --- and a rule written about fitted floors has nothing to read.
What we can report is cross-entropy at each channel's best cell, which is a
different and weaker quantity and is labelled as one throughout.
On it the prediction half-holds: English is the most expensive channel per
theorem, as predicted, but surface Lean is the \emph{cheapest} rather than the
middle, so the ordering
\(\mathrm{NL} > \mathrm{surface} > \mathrm{term}\) is non-monotone and is
reported as the negative result the registration said it would be.
\emph{(iii) One exponent inequality is refuted and one is supported, and they
must not be reported as one verdict.}
\(\alpha_{\mathrm{surface}} > \alpha_{\mathrm{NL}}\) is refuted.
Both arms route to a joint fit, so the two numbers are the same quantity
measured the same way, and under the Laplace posterior their \(90\%\) intervals
are disjoint: English begins at \num{sweep/nl/alphalo} where surface has
already ended at \num{sweep/surf/alphahi}.
A \num{sweep/bootstrapdraws}-resample bootstrap agrees, and the way it agrees
is worth one clause.
Its medians reproduce both arms --- \num{sweep/surf/bootalpha} against
surface's \num{sweep/surf/flatalpha}, \num{sweep/nl/bootalpha} against
English's \num{sweep/nl/flatalpha} --- but its resampling distribution on the
English arm is \emph{bimodal}, with an empty gap separating two solutions.
The better-fitting one holds \num{sweep/nl/bootmode1share}\% of draws at
\(R^2\) \num{sweep/nl/bootmode1rsq} and sits at
\num{sweep/nl/bootmode1alpha} \([\num{sweep/nl/bootmode1lo},
\num{sweep/nl/bootmode1hi}]\), reproducing the Laplace fit and disjoint from
surface;
the other is a degenerate basin at \(R^2\) \num{sweep/nl/bootmode2rsq} in which
the data exponent collapses toward zero and roams two orders of magnitude.
We rank by fit rather than by how many draws a mode holds, and name a principal
solution only where the two orderings agree and the fits separate --- which
they do here and do not on the term arm.
Surface is unimodal at \num{sweep/surf/bootmode1alpha}
\([\num{sweep/surf/bootmode1lo}, \num{sweep/surf/bootmode1hi}]\), a reported
fact rather than an absence, and the reason its two interval routes never
disagreed.
Pooled into one interval those two solutions look like a single wide one that
overlaps surface;
separated, the principal mode is disjoint from surface as the Laplace route
says.
Surface itself is unimodal.
We name the route and the shape because a quantile summary cannot show a gap:
pooled, this arm's interval reads as honest width, and only the resampling
histogram distinguishes one uncertain solution from two confident ones.
The result does not rest on the priors, which point the other way --- the
per-channel priors pull surface up and English down, that is, toward the
registered inequality --- and dropping them widens the gap rather than closing
it.
It does not rest on the parameter convention either: surface is last on the
total axis and last on the non-embedding axis (\cref{tab:sweep}).
\(\alpha_{\mathrm{term}} > \alpha_{\mathrm{surface}}\) is supported, and the
support is prior-free on both parameter conventions.

\emph{The bootstrap is reported beside that verdict, not as a defeater.}
Resampling this arm returns \num{sweep/term/bootmodes} separated solutions
rather than one uncertain estimate --- \num{sweep/term/bootmode2alpha} and
\num{sweep/term/bootmode1alpha}, an order of magnitude apart with no draws
between them --- and the more populous, at \num{sweep/term/bootmode2share}\% of
draws, is the \emph{worse} fit: \(R^2\) \num{sweep/term/bootmode2rsq} against
\num{sweep/term/bootmode1rsq}.
Ranked by fit, as the rule requires and as the English arm's split is also
read, the better solution sits at \num{sweep/term/bootmode1alpha}
\([\num{sweep/term/bootmode1lo}, \num{sweep/term/bootmode1hi}]\) and reproduces
the prior-free Laplace fit to within its own width --- the same agreement
English shows, on the one channel whose functional form is otherwise refused.
The pooled median, \num{sweep/term/bootalpha}, sits in the worse mode and is
not this arm's exponent;
it is what a summary statistic returns when it is asked to average two
answers.
What the rule declines to do here is \emph{designate}.
The two fits do not separate cleanly enough to name a principal solution
(\num{sweep/term/bootfitseparated} on the separation flag, against
\num{sweep/nl/bootfitseparated} for English), so we report both and rest the
verdict on the Laplace route and the flat fit rather than on choosing a mode.
Had the populous mode been the right one the inequality would reverse.
That is why this reads \emph{supported} and not \emph{established}, and it is
the honest width of the claim.
The implied fibre dimensions \(d = 4/\alpha\) are
\num{sweep/term/dimne}, \num{sweep/surf/dimne} and \num{sweep/nl/dimne} on the
non-embedding axis, and \num{sweep/term/dim}, \num{sweep/surf/dim} and
\num{sweep/nl/dim} on the total axis.
% The two axes used to ORDER term and English differently, and this sentence
% used to say so.  Under the prior in force they agree — term is smallest on
% both — so the disagreement is gone and citing it would be citing a fact the
% store no longer holds.  Both axes are still reported, for the reason that
% never depended on the disagreement.
Both are reported because neither answers the question alone: the three
vocabularies are \(8\times\) apart, so at the bottom of the ladder the
embedding matrix is a large and \emph{channel-dependent} share of total \(N\),
and a cross-channel dimension read on the total axis is partly a comparison of
tokenizers.
They now agree on the ordering, which they did not under the superseded prior;
what they still disagree about is the size of each dimension, and by most on
English and least on surface --- that is, in the order of the three vocabulary
sizes, which is what the correction is a correction for.
\emph{(iv) and (v) are not yet answerable}: the cross-check needs E2, which has
not run, and the dial test needs the synthetic arm.
\emph{(vi) is honoured}: no number above is read as an entropy.

\paragraph{Both exponents, and what the second one is worth.}
The registration predicts no \(\beta\), so what follows is observation rather
than confirmation --- but a scaling law is two exponents and two amplitudes,
and a section reporting one of the four leaves a reader unable to evaluate
\(L(N,D)\) at all.
With \(n = N/10^{6}\) parameters and \(d = D/10^{9}\) delivered tokens, and
\(H\) in nats per theorem:
% One law per line.  Three on one line overflowed the text block and truncated
% the English law mid-term in the PDF --- a silent overfull \hbox, which is a
% warning LaTeX gives and nobody reads.  Checked by looking at the rendered
% page, which is the only check that catches it.
\begin{align*}
\text{term:}\quad H &= \num{sweep/term/ampa}\, n^{-\num{sweep/term/alpha}}
   + \num{sweep/term/ampb}\, d^{-\num{sweep/term/beta}}, \\
\text{surface:}\quad H &= \num{sweep/surf/ampa}\, n^{-\num{sweep/surf/alpha}}
   + \num{sweep/surf/ampb}\, d^{-\num{sweep/surf/beta}}, \\
\text{English:}\quad H &= \num{sweep/nl/ampa}\, n^{-\num{sweep/nl/alpha}}
   + \num{sweep/nl/ampb}\, d^{-\num{sweep/nl/beta}}.
\end{align*}
No irreducible term appears because none is fitted: \(E\) is not identified
over this grid and is fixed at zero under \(f = 1\).

\emph{Three readings, in decreasing order of how much they are worth.}
The ordering \(\beta_{\mathrm{term}} > \beta_{\mathrm{NL}} >
\beta_{\mathrm{surface}}\) matches the \(\alpha\) ordering, which was not
predicted and is not evidence for anything the registration asked.
The three posteriors are all far tighter than the priors they started from
(\(\num{sweep/term/betashrink}\), \(\num{sweep/surf/betashrink}\) and
\(\num{sweep/nl/betashrink}\) of the prior width), so all three are
measurements rather than priors read back --- which is worth saying because a
superseded prior on this same arm returned exactly that.
And term's \(\beta\) is \emph{not} the steepest in this literature:
\num{sweep/lit/term/betasteeper} of the \num{sweep/lit/count} published fits
are steeper, all of them programming languages from
\citet{yang2026codescaling}, whose range is also what centres term's own
prior.
Its \(\alpha\), by contrast, is the steepest of the set --- the same count is
\num{sweep/lit/term/alphasteeper} --- though not by a margin the interval
resolves: the two nearest published exponents, Go at
\num{sweep/lit/yang2026codescaling_go/alpha} and JavaScript at
\num{sweep/lit/yang2026codescaling_javascript/alpha}, both lie inside term's
own \(90\%\) interval.
\emph{Both statements come with the same caveat, and on \(\beta\) it is the
larger one.}
This grid varies \(D\) at fixed tokens-per-update, so the three data rungs are
also three update counts and \(\beta\) is a joint tokens-and-optimisation
exponent on every arm;
it may be set against a published \(\beta\) only in so far as that study's data
axis is collinear the same way, and no extrapolation in \(D\) is licensed,
because extrapolating \(D\) here extrapolates the step count with it.
Term's row carries a second warning that the other two do not:
its law misses its own cells by \num{sweep/term/relrms}\% against
\num{sweep/surf/relrms}\% and \num{sweep/nl/relrms}\%, so its \(\beta\) is what
a forced Chinchilla fit returns on a channel measured outside the family, not
that channel's data exponent.

\subsection{E2 --- the matched per-theorem accounting}
\label{sec:experiments:cap}

The second instrument prices the same quantity with one model per channel rather
than a grid, in two stages.

\paragraph{The gate.}
Before committing training compute we run the comparison at small scale under
the \emph{stock} base model with no fine-tuning:
\(200\) matched pairs, conditioned identically, per-theorem cross-entropy on
both channels.
The language side is scored under a \emph{ladder} of open-weights scorers rather
than one model, in bits per byte over the identical detokenised stream, under a
prompt pre-registered before scoring, because every degree of freedom in the
prompt inflates \(\CE_{\mathrm{NL}}\) in the direction that flatters the paper.
The ladder makes the misfit auditable:
cross-entropy differences identify KL differences exactly, so each rung
certifies a residual reported alongside the gap.
We proceed to the arms only if the gap has the predicted sign under the
strongest scorer and the formal share is below one half;
if either fails, this paper reports the instrument, the population audit and the
negative result.
The gate costs a few GPU-hours; the arms it gates cost weeks.

\paragraph{The arms.}
Three arms, one base model, one theorem set, the protocol of
\cref{sec:method:protocol}:
the language arm fine-tuned to produce the worked solution, the surface arm the
proof-assistant source, the term arm the serialised kernel term, each
conditioned on the byte-identical English statement.
We publish the length ledger the gap must clear on the same set, because the
formal channel is the \emph{longer} encoding and the comparison is only
interesting because of it.
On this population we can also price the one noise term that is counted rather
than inferred:
the freedom in \emph{which} accepted term realises a goal
(\cref{sec:method:identity}).

\tbm{E2: per-theorem cross-entropy per arm --- median, quartiles and bootstrap
CIs on the pre-declared primary estimand, on the proof-type human-authored
stratum, other strata separately --- with each arm's learning curve and stopping
point, the scorer-ladder table with certified pairwise misfit residuals, the
formal-to-language length ratios by question type, and the sampled accept-set
entropy with its censoring above \(\log k\) stated; instrument: the three
fine-tuning runs, the single scoring routine of \cref{sec:method:protocol}, and
the sampling harness with the kernel as accept oracle}

\paragraph{What this comparison is, and is not.}
Translating a natural-language proof into a kernel term is not an
information-preserving recoding:
the language proof omits steps a formal proof must supply, and the formal proof
omits motivation the language proof carries.
This is an accounting of two learning problems over one theorem set, not a
recoding theorem.
The direction matters:
a channel that must supply \emph{more} detail and still costs \emph{fewer} nats
is the interesting case, and it is the case we predict.

\subsection{E3 --- rebuilding the entropy comparison}
\label{sec:experiments:fig3}

The predecessor to this work reported a histogram comparing per-position
predictive entropy on serialised kernel terms against natural-language corpora,
and three reviewers and the area chair independently named it its strongest
evidence.
It is not a matched comparison.
Seven mismatches, in descending order of how much each alone could explain the
gap:
(1) \textbf{task asymmetry} --- formal positions conditioned on the full goal
type, language positions unconditioned next-token prediction on running text;
(2) \textbf{no fine-tuning on the language side}, whose bars came from an
off-the-shelf model while the formal bar came from a model trained on its
channel;
(3) \textbf{different models entirely}, of different sizes;
(4) \textbf{a mislabelled corpus} --- the bar reported as ``arXiv abstracts''
was drawn from a dataset whose only text field is the full paper body, the
requested abstract field not existing;
(5) \textbf{a mis-attributed checkpoint} --- captioned as from-scratch, but the
recovered run record shows a warm-started configuration;
(6) \textbf{unverified holdout} --- the training pack and the pack the entropy
was read from are different artefacts, the latter flagged degenerate in the
project's own records;
and (7) \textbf{a non-random sample} --- the first \(4{,}000\) rows in pack
order, which is blocked by source corpus.
The quantity was also not what the surrounding text implied:
predictive entropy \(H(p_t)\) never reads the target token, so it measures model
confidence rather than loss.
We rebuild it at the current pin as a matched measurement:
one base model, both channels fine-tuned on their own data to comparable
convergence, both scored as conditional generation given the same statement,
sampled uniformly, with the quantity stated explicitly.

\todoFIG{HEADLINE. Per-theorem cost across the three arms on one nats axis:
distributions, not bars, with the length ledger alongside so the reader sees the
formal channel paying more tokens for fewer nats. The three fitted floors of E1,
converted per theorem, are marked on the same axis --- both instruments in one
picture. The scorer ladder overlays the language arm as a band with its
certified residuals annotated, and a non-neural compression floor is printed so
that ``low'' has a reference point that is not another model.}

\subsection{E4 --- the free-running arm, as robustness}
\label{sec:experiments:freerun}

Every measurement above is teacher-forced on a fixed corpus.
As a robustness leg we re-run the accounting on the model's \emph{own}
distribution:
sampling from \(\pi_\theta\) makes \(\KL{P}{\pi_\theta} = 0\) by construction and
\(H_\theta(\mathrm{NL})\) an ordinary Monte-Carlo expectation, with the paired
formal side supplied by a statement autoformaliser \(\phi\) from
\cref{tab:roster};
this also answers a standing objection to the predecessor, that every
measurement in it was teacher-forced.
Three caveats are printed with the leg rather than left for a reviewer.
The estimand changes --- this arm measures one model's output distribution, not
the corpus limit, so it cannot carry the headline.
\(H_\theta\) is gameable downward and can collapse, so we report across
temperatures with a degeneracy check.
And \(\phi\) selects, because rows where it fails or the kernel rejects are
dropped and the selection is on formalisability, exactly the variable under
study, so we report the drop rate and the bound on both the kept and the full
set.
\(\phi\) supplies the paired formal side; it does not tighten the inequality.

\tbm{free-running outcome: \(H_\theta\) across temperatures with degeneracy
diagnostics, the autoformalisation drop rate, and the bound on the kept and the
full set; instrument: the sampling harness over the trained arms, the
autoformaliser of \cref{tab:roster}, and the kernel checker}

\subsection{Threats to validity}
\label{sec:experiments:threats}

\emph{The population is selected, and we publish the cascade.}
Every stage of the join removes rows, and the removals are not random with
respect to difficulty.

\emph{Contamination has no internal alarm.}
The English side of every roster corpus is public and inside open pretraining
mixes, so a scorer can have memorised held-out rows;
memorisation drives a measured \(\CE\) below \(H\) and voids \cref{eq:cehkl}
silently, and no statistic computed from the scorer alone detects it.
The near-duplicate scan of R7 is the mitigation and cannot be a proof for a
closed pretraining mix.
The nats cap is unaffected; the absolute reading and the fraction are what
contamination can bias.

\emph{Censoring, and a conditioning we inherit.}
The loss side is blind above the context cap, where the reference cannot be
represented and its cross-entropy is undefined.
On the current evaluation split this is severe:
the split contains essentially no witnesses at the cap, so it is conditioned on
short proofs and every per-theorem number inherits that conditioning.
\tbm{over-cap fraction of the library against that of the evaluation split, and
the excluded mass; instrument: the witness-length census re-run with the
serialiser the tokenizer is paired with}

\emph{One arm's resampling distribution is bimodal, and a pooled interval hides
it.}
On the English arm a minority of resamples land in a basin where both exponents
collapse to zero and the amplitude terms absorb the data.
Pooling them with the principal mode produces an interval about four times the
Laplace posterior's, wide enough to overlap surface and to look like ordinary
uncertainty at any quantile summary;
the modes are separated by a range containing no draws at all.
We report the better-fitting mode, which reproduces the Laplace interval
closely.
\emph{Better-fitting, not more populous}: the two criteria happen to agree on
the English arm and disagree on the term arm, where the majority solution is
the poorer fit, so a rule that ranked modes by how many draws they hold would
have named the wrong one there.
The same check found the term arm bimodal as well, on a different pair of
solutions, and the surface arm unimodal --- which is why surface is the arm on
which the two interval routes agree, and why it serves as the control here
rather than only in the ordering.
One coincidence we report without explaining: the rejected mode on both bimodal
arms sits at the same exponent to the precision we quote
(\num{sweep/nl/bootmode2alpha} and \num{sweep/term/bootmode2alpha}), on
different data and with different second parameters and fit qualities.
It may be an artefact of the optimiser under a flat prior rather than anything
about the channels;
we have not established which, and it bears on nothing above.
We found all of this by plotting the resampling distributions rather than
summarising them;
every quantile summary involved was correct and none of them showed it.
The refutation does not rest on any of this: the priors point \emph{toward} the
inequality we refute, and dropping them widens the gap rather than closing it.

\emph{One pin, one base model, one seed.}
Every distributional statement here is about that configuration;
the pin and the snapshot are recorded in \cref{app:ledger}.
